chapter_theme: Teaching (உபதேசம்): the Lord comes down as the guru and burns away the soul's impurity, which is beginningless like the soul; through grace and Siva-yoga the freed come to rest in Sivam, in a state of stillness, 'sleep' and silence that cannot be told. The means offered are the guru's form, name and word and Nandi's feet.
structure_note: The verses form an andhadi: each opens with the word that ends the one before (களிம்பறுத்தானே, களிம்பறுத்தான்; பதியே, பதி; and so on). The movement is from the guru's descent and the removal of malas (113 to 120), through Siva-yoga and the siddhas (121 to 129), the dance and the gain of those who worship it (130 to 132), images of union (133 to 137), to the feet, the guru and Nandi as refuge (138 to 142).

113.reading: Coming down from the sky, taking a body to answer my deeds, setting his cool feet on my head as a guard, melting me from within and showing me in the eye an incomparable bliss, he cut away the verdigris.
113.nuance: களிம்பு is the green tarnish on copper; tradition takes it as the soul's root impurity (ஆணவம்), and the verse as the Lord descending as guru. வினைக்கு ஈடாய் may mean the body he took suits the disciple's deeds, so that the Lord meets the soul in a form it can receive.

114.reading: He cut away the verdigris, our Nandi with the eye in his forehead; cutting it, he opened the eye of grace, showed a radiant light that tarnish cannot touch, and set coral in crystal: he is the Lord.
114.nuance: பளிங்கில் பவளம் பதித்தான் (set coral in crystal) is symbolic: commonly read as the red Lord shining in the soul once it is clear like crystal. பதி, the verse's last word, is both 'Lord' and the first word of the next verse.

115.reading: Of the three named Pati, Pasu and Pasam, Pasu and Pasam are beginningless like Pati; Pasu and Pasam cannot go and reach Pati, but when Pati draws near, Pasu and Pasam do not remain.
115.nuance: The verse states the Saiva Siddhanta triad of Lord, soul and bond, and makes all three without beginning. The last line is traditionally read as the end of the soul's bondage (its being a பசு, a bound creature), not of the soul itself; the verse alone does not make that distinction. Approach is one-way: the soul cannot reach the Lord, the Lord must come.

116.reading: Like fire that rises from bamboo, Nandi, the king who has made his home in the temple called this body, removes the three malas more tenderly than a mother and rises as a sun that is the water of compassion.
116.nuance: Fire latent in bamboo, which comes out by friction, is the Lord hidden in the body. The body is called a temple (மெய் எனும் கோயில்), not a filthy frame. The last line mixes images: a sun that is the water (தோயம்) of mercy; tradition takes it as grace that both burns impurity and cools.

117.reading: As a sunstone does not burn the cotton around it until it stands in the sun's presence, and then burns it, so the malas end before the sun appears.
117.nuance: The sunstone is commonly taken as the soul, the cotton as the malas and the sun as the Lord or the guru. The point is that the soul has the power to burn its impurity only in the Lord's presence.

118.reading: Making known that the malas are five, he removed them in grace; Nandi in that common hall, who is Sadasiva of the five stations, cleared away the five domains and, knowing them, desired the good within.
118.nuance: Five malas are traditionally ஆணவம், கன்மம், மாயை, மாயேயம் and திரோதாயி, though the verse does not name them. தலங்கள் ஐந்து (five stations) and புலங்கள் (domains, senses) are unclear, and the last line is obscure.

119.reading: When awareness, hanging on the five senses, was lost like water sunk in depths with no outlet, and was as if it had perished within awareness, the supreme guru makes known the sign.
119.nuance: நான்றது (hung on, depended on) and நீர் ஆழம் (deep water) are the key images. அறிவு அறிவுள்ளே அழிந்தது is hard: perhaps the soul's knowing swallowed by the senses, or a positive merging. குறி (sign, mark) is left unexplained.

120.reading: Like the swan that parts milk from water, he alone, eternally, in the solitary hall, makes what is lodged in the many fiery faculties into seeds that have touched the fire and will not sprout into the seven births.
120.nuance: A roasted seed does not sprout: deeds burnt by grace no longer yield births. Who parts milk from water is not stated; it may be the Lord, the guru or the discerning soul. ஆமேவு, the opening, is obscure.

121.reading: Having destroyed the seed, with the pure turiya state arising strongly in waking, bonds cut, senses and life become one, they remain with the body as if dead: these are the Siva-yogis.
121.nuance: வியாக்கிரம் (literally tiger) is obscure; it is often taken as ஜாக்கிரம், the waking state, giving turiya in waking. 'Dead with the body' is taken as dead to the senses while alive. Sengalvaraya notes a parallel in Kandar Alangaram 19.

122.reading: Siva-yoga is to know the conscient and the non-conscient, enter the yoga of tapas, become one's own light, not take to false yoga, and go to his abode; Nandi of the nava-yoga gave it to us.
122.nuance: சித்து, அசித்து are the conscient (souls) and the non-conscient (matter). அவயோகம் is read as wrong or lower yoga. நவயோகம் may mean 'the new yoga' or 'nine yogas'; the text doesn't decide.

123.reading: He gave the truth that he is himself the whole world; he gave the world the gods do not know; he gave the holy feet that dance in the sacred hall; he gave the open space of grace in great bliss.
123.nuance: The anaphora on அளித்தான் (he gave) builds a list of gifts that rise from knowledge to bliss. Sengalvaraya notes a parallel in Tirumurugatruppadai 293.

124.reading: Those who see clearly how space went into space and mingled, how sweetness went into sweetness and subsided, how light went into light and was absorbed: they are the Siva-siddhas.
124.nuance: அளி can be honey, the bee or grace; whichever, the pattern is like merging into like. Three images of union without remainder.

125.reading: Siddhas are those who have seen Sivaloka here, who hold within them sound and sound's end; eternal, stainless, free of affliction, the far-supreme freed ones, their release begins from the thirty-six.
125.nuance: சத்தமும் சத்த முடிவும் are taken as nada and nadanta. முப்பத்தாறு is the thirty-six tattvas. 'Sivaloka here' (இங்கே) makes release something seen in this life.

126.reading: Taking the thirty-six as the rungs of a ladder to release, entering the inner light of incomparable bliss, seeing the unspeakable Sivam and becoming clear, they remained settled in that state.
126.nuance: The tattvas, which elsewhere unfold the world downward from Siva, are here climbed upward as rungs. Sengalvaraya notes parallels in Kandar Anubhuti 47 and Kandar Alangaram 55.

127.reading: They remained having become Sivam and everything; they remained watching all of Siva's acts; they remained knowing the nature of the three times; they remained in the idleness that came when the loss had come.
127.nuance: சோம்பு (idleness) is turned to praise: the stillness of one who has nothing left to do. இழவு (loss) is not said: loss of self, of the world, or of striving.

128.reading: The idle ones dwell in pure space, lie in pure space; their awareness is where the Veda ends, and what they saw is sleep within that Veda.
128.nuance: The Kural lists sloth and sleep among the marks of those headed for ruin (605); Tirumular makes the same words name the freed. சுருதி முடிந்திடம் (where the Veda ends) is Vedanta, and சுருதிக்கண் தூக்கம் rest in it. The inversion is deliberate, but it is about stillness in Sivam, not worldly work.

129.reading: Sleeping, they saw Sivaloka within themselves; sleeping, Siva-yoga within themselves; sleeping, Siva-bhoga within themselves; how could that state be told?
129.nuance: The world, the union and the enjoyment of Siva are all found inside (தம்முள்ளே). The sleep is a sleep with awareness; Sengalvaraya notes Tiruppugazh 757, 'those who sleep with awareness'.

130.reading: However far one's knowing reaches, so far the first Hara gives grace; he who dances in the matchless hall for Uma to see is a ruby redder than the red sky, a rich flame.
130.nuance: The first line makes grace proportioned to the seeker's capacity. The red sky and ruby fix Siva's colour as red, as in 114.

131.reading: Within the ruby an emerald light, within the ruby an emerald mansion: what a gain did they gain who cherished and worshipped the holy dance in the hall of finest gold!
131.nuance: Ruby and emerald are traditionally Siva and Uma, the green one within the red. ஆணிப்பொன் is gold of the finest touch. The last line's question is answered in 132.

132.reading: They gained in this world the great path that does not part from him, the great fruit of not being born, the great attainment that does not part from that hall, and the greatness of not speaking with the world.
132.nuance: உலகுடன் பேசாப் பெருமை may be silence, or freedom from worldly converse and ties. All four gains are had 'in the world' (உலகில்).

133.reading: Who but our Lord knows greatness and smallness, and knows the hard and the easy? Those who, in one birth (or in one-pointedness), drew the five within like a tortoise and heard both, remained without flaw.
133.nuance: The third line nearly repeats Kural 126 (ஒருமையுள் ஆமைபோல் ஐந்தடக்கல்), where ஒருமை is usually taken as 'one birth'; here it may keep that sense or mean one-pointedness. இருமையும் கேட்டு is unclear: 'heard both' (this world and the next, or both teachings), or, if கேட்டு is a misreading of கெட்டு, 'with duality destroyed'.

134.reading: Like ghee mixed in pure milk, those who feel beyond words what the noble teacher of waveless mind speaks, once their body falls here, become the reality mixed in the shoreless light.
134.nuance: ஆரியன் here is the noble teacher. Ghee in milk is present throughout yet unseen until churned; it may be the Lord in the soul or the teaching in the hearer. சத்து (being, reality) is what the knower becomes.

135.reading: If the five beginning with sound settle back by their own path, where else is there for the conscient to join except the Conscient? In pure space flame joins flame; grasp this meaning and be ruled, as in water.
135.nuance: சித்துக்குச் சித்து: the conscient soul's only home is the conscient Lord. ஆண்டுகொள் அப்பிலே is obscure; அப்பு (water) leads into the salt image of 136.

136.reading: As salt, named and given form by the sun's heat on the water's sharpness, becomes one again in the water it meets, so, it is said, the soul subsides into Sivam.
136.nuance: The salt was always of the water and returns to it. The image suggests non-difference; Siddhanta tradition reads it as union in which the soul does not perish, which the verse alone does not settle. அடங்கும் (subsides, is contained) is milder than 'is lost'.

137.reading: In the great universe that subsides, the atom-worlds go and find no room; is there anything other than this? If you see the shore of the life that stands in each body, it is the holy feet of the one who stood firm.
137.nuance: கடம் (pot) stands for the body. The first two lines are obscure; the plain sense of the last two is that the limit of every soul is the Lord's feet.

138.reading: Examine it and the holy feet are Sivam; think on it and the holy feet are Sivaloka; speak of it and the holy feet are the path to travel; the holy feet are refuge for those clear within.
138.nuance: The feet are at once the Lord, his world and the way there. தஞ்சம் is refuge. The 'clear within' (உள் தெளிவார்) leads into 139, which defines clarity.

139.reading: Clarity is seeing the guru's holy form, uttering the guru's holy name, hearing the guru's holy words and thinking on the guru's form.
139.nuance: The four acts engage eye, tongue, ear and mind. Clarity (தெளிவு) is not reached by argument here but by devotion to the guru.

140.reading: Of themselves the five senses come under one's control; of themselves they go into his control; of themselves they turn their channels inward, once one has met our Lord alone.
140.nuance: தன்வசம் can mean 'in one's own power' or 'in his (the Lord's) power', and the first two lines may differ on just that. மடைமாறும் (the sluice turns) is an irrigation image: the senses' flow is redirected. The key word is தானே: the control is not achieved by effort but follows from meeting the Lord.

141.reading: What one meets is Nandi's pair of holy feet; what one thinks on is Nandi's red holy form; what one praises in truth is Nandi's name; what stands within the mind is Nandi's golden feet.
141.nuance: சந்திப்பது picks up the last word of 140. Nandi is both Siva and the guru-lineage; the verse leaves them as one.

142.reading: Those who placed our meritorious Nandi, who gives understanding, within their understanding became meritorious; with their eyes overflowing at the Lord's dance and the Veda praising, they went and reached the sky.
142.nuance: போதம் (understanding) is played on: Nandi gives it, and is placed in it. விண் may be heaven or the space of Sivam the earlier verses speak of.

links.note: Tirumular's third line nearly repeats the Kural's: ஒருமையுள் ஆமைபோல் ... ஐந்து அடக்கி. The Kural makes the restraint a protection through seven births (எழுமையும்); Tirumular's version ends instead with those who 'heard both' (இருமையும்) and stand flawless.

Both use the bird that drinks milk and leaves water. The Naladiyar makes it the wise learning only what is fitting; Tirumular makes it the parting that turns deeds into seeds that cannot sprout into births.

The Naladiyar makes guarding the craving that enters through the five gates the effort that reaches release; Tirumular says the five come under control of themselves (தானே) once one has met the Lord. Restraint is a cause in one, a result in the other.
The Kural says those who reach the Lord's feet cross the sea of births; Tirumular makes the feet the refuge, the path and the goal itself.
Both call the body the Lord's temple: 116 where Nandi lives like fire in bamboo, 725 where Tirumular, who once thought the body a defect, found the Lord inside it and so tends it.

The Naladiyar calls the body a stinking cart that only the ignorant adorn and praise; Tirumular calls it the temple where the Lord dwells. The conflict holds if கோயில் is read as giving the body worth, not only as locating the Lord in it.
1924 counts the thirty-six tattvas as they unfold from bindu and nada; 126 climbs the same thirty-six as the rungs of a ladder to release.

The Kural counts sloth and sleep among the pleasure-boats of those bound for ruin; Tirumular gives the same words (சோம்பு, தூக்கம்) to the freed resting in Sivam. The Kural's verdict is on worldly duty; Tirumular names a state beyond it.

113 says the Lord came down, took a body suited to the disciple's deeds (வினைக்கீடாய் மெய்க்கொண்டு) and cut away the verdigris. 1527 names the condition and the form: when the two deeds stand balanced (இருவினை நேரொப்பில்) grace comes as the guru (குருவென வந்து) and the three malas end. The pairing turns 113's single scene into the doctrine of when and how the guru comes.

114 says the Lord, once the tarnish was cut, set coral in crystal (பளிங்கிற் பவளம் பதித்தான்): the red Lord shows in the cleared soul. Kural 706 uses the same property of crystal, that it shows what is set beside it (அடுத்தது காட்டும் பளிங்கு), for the face showing the heart. One image serves both a mystic claim and a courtier's rule for reading faces.

115 states the triad: pasu and pasam are beginningless like pati, cannot reach pati, and do not remain when pati draws near (பதியணுகிற் பசு பாசம் நில்லாவே). Thiruppugazh 1218 turns the doctrine into a plea that pati, pasu and pasam be set apart each from each without stain (பதிபசு பாசம் ஆனவை கசடற வேறு வேறுசெய்). The same terms pass from Tirumular's statement to Arunagiri's prayer for the discrimination it implies.

116 calls the body a temple where Nandi has made his home (மெய்யெனும் கோயில் இருந்து குடிகொண்ட கோன்) and is kinder than a mother (தாயினும்). 1728 has the same three words: the body taken as temple (கோயில்கொண்டு), the five dwelling there (குடிகொண்ட), the Master entering as if taken into a mother (தாயில் கொண்டாற்போல்). Both make the indwelling Lord domestic and maternal rather than the body something to despise.

117 says the sunstone does not burn the cotton around it except in the sun's presence (சூரியன் சந்நிதியிற் சுடுமாறுபோல்), so the malas end when the sun appears. 1653 uses the same stone: the sunstone that sees the sun takes the form of fire (கதிர்கண்ட காந்தம் கனலின் வடிவாம்). In 117 the stone shows that grace, not the soul, does the burning; in 1653 it shows the soul taking the form of what it faces.

117 ends: before the sun's appearing the malas are gone (சூரியன் தோற்றமுன் அற்ற மலங்களே). 2245 says the bonds and the three malas are let go by the ray that is Siva (சிவனான கதிராலே), the maddening darkness running off. Both make the removal of impurity the work of a sun that is the Lord, not of the soul's effort.

118 says the Lord made known that the malas are five and removed them by grace (மலங்கள்ஐந் தாமென மாற்றி அருளி). 2059 says those who bow at the feet of the Lord wither the five malas that well up (ஊற்றிடும் ஐம்மலம்). Both count the malas as five, against the more common three of 115-117, and set their removal at the Lord's side.

119 says awareness, caught in the five senses, was lost as if it had perished within awareness (அறிவுஅறி வுள்ளே அழிந்தது போல) until the guru makes the sign known. Thiruppugazh 714 asks for the knowing that knows within knowing (அறிவுள் அறியும் அறிவு) to see the feet no one else could know. The same doubled அறிவு names the loss in 119 and the gift in Arunagiri.

119 ends with the supreme guru making the sign known (குறியறிவிப்பான் குருபரன்). 2580 says those who do not know the sign (குறியறியாதவர்) of putting away both knowing and not-knowing cannot grasp Siva. Read together, 2580 says what the sign is that 119's guru gives.

120 says the guru makes what lodges in the fiery faculties into seeds that have touched fire (எரிசார்ந்த வித்து), so they cannot sprout into the seven births. 1964's riddle has a man who roasts the seed and eats it (வித்துச் சுட்டு உண்பான்), and so knows no harvest. The roasted seed is release in 120 and waste in 1964; the image carries opposite values in the two places.

121 says the Siva-yogis remain with the body as if dead (உடம்பொடு செத்திட்டிருப்பார்). 1907 says those who, still in the world, have died to the three malas (செத்தார் இருந்தார் செகத்தில் திரிமலம்) become Siva and are the siddhas. Both define the goal as a death undergone while living.

122 says Siva-yoga is to enter the yoga of tapas and become one's own light (தவயோகத்துள் புக்குத் தன்னொளி தானாய்). 1638 ends the same way: within tapas the light of the way becomes one's own light (தவத்திடை யாறொளி தன்னொளி யாமே). 1638 adds the means, the sword of understanding and the five turned back, to 122's definition.

125 says the siddhas have seen Sivaloka here and are stainless freed ones (நிமலர் ... முத்தர்). 2526 defines them again: siddhas are those who have seen Siva (சித்தர் சிவத்தைக் கண்டவர்), freed ones rooted at the root of release. The two verses, far apart, give the same definition of a siddha.

126 makes the thirty-six (tattvas) the rungs of a ladder to release (முப்பதும் ஆறும் படிமுத்தி ஏணியாய்). 2020 says Nandi made known the nature of the thirty-six and then stood beyond them (ஆறாறுக்கு அப்புறம் ஆகி நின்றானே). The ladder of 126 needs the guru's teaching of 2020 to be climbed, and its top is beyond the ladder.

126 counts thirty and six as a ladder to release; 154 counts thirty and thirty and thirty-six who live in the walled temple of the body (முப்பதும் முப்பதும் முப்பத்தறுவரும்) and run off when it falls. The same number names the tattvas that lift the soul in 126 and the tenants who desert the dying body in 154.

Kural 339 says death is like sleep and birth like waking from it (உறங்குவது போலும் சாக்காடு). 129 says that sleeping (தூங்கி) the siddhas saw Sivaloka, Siva-yoga and Siva-bhoga within themselves, and 121 calls them dead with the body. Tirumular uses the Kural's sleep-as-death for a sleep from which no waking into birth follows.

129 says sleeping they saw Siva-yoga within and Siva-bhoga within (சிவ யோகமும் ... சிவ போகமும் தம்முள்ளே). 1491 says both yoga and enjoyment come to yogis (யோகமும் போகமும் யோகியர்க்காகுமால்). 1491 sets out as doctrine the pairing of yoga and bhoga that 129 finds in the siddha's sleep.

130 says however far one's knowing reaches, so far the first Hara gives grace (எவ்வாறு காண்பான் அறிவு தனக்கெல்லை அவ்வாறு அருட்செய்வன்). 2005 calls him the One perceived as far as one contemplates him (உன்னும் அளவில் உணரும் ஒருவனை). Both make the Lord's self-giving measured to the seeker's capacity.

133 says those who drew the five within like a tortoise (ஆமைபோல் உள்ஐந்து அடக்கி) remained without flaw. 2158 has the five drawing in within the tortoise (ஆமை அகத்தினில் அஞ்சம் அடங்கிடும்) when the silent and spoken letter meet. In 133 the drawing-in is the seeker's restraint; in 2158 it follows the mantra.

134 says those who feel the guru's word beyond words, when the body falls, merge with the shoreless light like ghee mixed in pure milk (புரைஅற்ற பாலினுள் நெய்கலந்தாற்போல்). 2639 uses ghee in milk (பாலினுள் நெய்யும்) for the Lord present unseen in everything. The same pair names the soul dissolving into the Lord in 134 and the Lord hidden in the world in 2639.

135 asks where the conscient can go except to the Conscient (சித்துக்குச் சித்தன்றி சேர்விடம் வேறுண்டோ) once the five beginning with sound settle back. 1907 says what the dead gain is to join pure consciousness (சித்தினைக் கூடிடில்). Both name the end as the conscient soul joining the Conscient.

136 says the soul subsides into Sivam as salt formed by the sun's heat becomes one again with the water (அப்பினிற் கூடியது ஒன்றாகுமாறுபோல்). 2945 opens with the Father joining like salt in water (அப்பினில் உப்பென அத்தன் அணைந்திட்டு). The two verses use the same image for union without remainder.

136 has salt made from water dissolving back into it, for the soul subsiding into Sivam. 491 runs the image the other way: the subtle body dissolved in the Supreme takes form again as sea-salt crystallizes (திரைக்கடல் உப்புத் திரண்டது போல) and is born. The same salt figures release in 136 and rebirth in 491.

139 places clarity in seeing the guru's form, saying his name, hearing his words and thinking of his form (தெளிவு குருவின் திருமேனி காண்டல்). 2119 gives the reason: worship of Siva alone gave the gods no way to become him, but worshipping the guru who shows the way makes union possible (குருவை வழிபடின் கூடலும் ஆமே).

140 says the five senses come under control of themselves (தானே புலன்ஐந்துந் தன்வசம் ஆயிடும்) once one meets the Lord alone. 1638 asks for effort: draw the sword of understanding and turn the five back so they do not stray (அஞ்சும் போகாமல் மறித்தால்). Read together, the effortless control of 140 follows meeting the Lord, while 1638's labour comes before it.

141 repeats 139's acts point by point with Nandi in place of the guru: meeting his feet, thinking of his red form (சிந்திப்பது நந்தி செய்ய திருமேனி), praising his name. The near-repeat identifies the guru of 139 with Nandi.
